title: Dex and the Decimal Delights
markdown:
The Whispering Willow Market did not wait to be introduced. It was already mid-chatter when Dex arrived, mind whirring like a clockmaker’s extra drawer, Biscuit trotting at his heel with a tail that treated every stall as a festival. A woman sold ribbons that changed colour if you told them the weather; Dex did not stop. He had promised himself Hale’s corner first.

Colours argued. Candied fruit sweetened the air; bread answered with warm earth. A boy went by with a paper cone of nuts and a frown at a chalkboard. They had come for peculiar treasures and found, at Dr. Hale’s stall, a puzzle that refused to sit still.

The stall overflowed. Sun-gem pebbles pulsed with their own light. Giggling glow-worms nested in glass jars like fallen stars that had decided to stay. Self-folding napkins snapped into swans if you flicked a wrist and then looked innocent. Dex’s eyes widened. Then the prices arrived and his brain knotted.

A small cloud in a bottle: *One cloud, 1.75.* Three plump berries, each the size of a ladybug: *Three berries, 2.50.* A whistle carved from a fallen meteor, which Dex suspected might laugh like a dragon: *Dragon’s Laugh Whistle, 3.25.*

“Good heavens, Biscuit,” Dex murmured, scratching until his spectacles nearly left. “How can a cloud be 1.75? Is it only partly a cloud, with a bit of fog mixed in?”

Biscuit offered a questioning ruff and a tilt. Dex’s brow crumpled. The inventive spark dimmed in the fog of the little dots.

Dr. Hale emerged from behind a tower of enchanted teacups, tweed jacket with more pockets than seemed polite, smile crinkling. “Having a spot of bother with the pricing?”

Dex nodded, a blush climbing. “How can something cost parts of a coin? What does point-seven-five of an apple even mean?”

Hale chuckled, wind-chimes. He picked up a perfectly round golden apple. “This is one. A whole. Undivided.” Then a pie, sliced into ten equal pieces. “One slice is one tenth, written .1. Two slices, .2. Seven, .7.” He tapped the little dot as if it were a door.

Dex looked from apple to pie to the sign: 1.75. He traced the numbers in the air. “So 1.75 is one whole… and then seven tenths? And the five?”

“Imagine the pie cut into a hundred crumbs,” Hale said. “Seventy-five of those crumbs is .75. The mark is a decimal point. It tells you we have left the whole numbers and started talking about parts. Useful for measuring. Useful for prices, so nobody tries to swap half a coin for a whole invention and call it even.”

The gears clicked. “The 1.75 is one coin and seventy-five hundredths of another. The 2.50 berries are two coins and a half. Not two and a half berries pretending to be prices.”

“Indeed.” Hale’s eyes twinkled. “Accuracy instead of a jumble.”

Dex pulled a notepad and a pencil stub. The stall became a sorting job. He lined the signs so the decimal points stood in a column, like buttons on the same coat. A jar of marbles that caught rainbows: 3.10. “Three coins and one tenth.” He moved the cloud bottle beside the berries and read them aloud to Biscuit, who did not need to shop but liked being included. Biscuit, sensing the shift from tangle to work, yipped and conducted the air with his tail. A napkin folded itself into a swan and then, perhaps embarrassed, into a slightly flatter swan.

A woman paused at the glow-worms, frowning at 4.50 as if the worms were half a joke. Dex tapped the point. “Four coins and fifty hundredths. Half a coin more than four.” She bought two jars and left smiling, which Hale counted as a different kind of accurate. Shoppers who had been murmuring over the dots now browsed without squinting. A sun-gem pebble at 0.75 sat clearly below the worms: no whole coin at all, only seventy-five hundredths. Dex pointed, triumphant, at a contraption that hummed and puffed lavender smoke. “9.99. Nearly ten. One hundredth short.” He almost reached for a tenth coin and then stopped, pleased with the almost.

Hale ruffled his hair and did not deliver a speech about the immense power of small numbers. He moved the 0.75 pebble to the front of the table so the smallest price could be seen first.

Dex looked at the market, still loud, still sweet. The dots were not fog mixed into clouds. They were a way to say *not quite a whole* without waving your hands. He wrote 1.75, 2.50, 3.25 in a column, lined up on the points, and the jumble sat down. Biscuit sat too, which was rarer. The next stall, if it used whole numbers only, would look suddenly shy.
